opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of the first big questions. With math and coding you have these well-established benchmarks and datasets where you can check whether an answer is right, so it's pretty clear what you're optimizing for. With browsing there wasn't really an equivalent, so we had to step back and ask what we actually wanted the model to be good at.

We grounded it in the kinds of tasks people actually struggle with online: questions where the answer is out there, but finding it means searching a lot of different sources, following leads, and piecing information together. The useful property is that these questions are hard to find answers to but easy to verify once you have the answer. That asymmetry matters a lot, because it gives you a clear signal for training even when the path to the answer is long and messy.

So a lot of the early work was building those datasets ourselves. We created tasks where we knew the ground truth, and the model had to do real research to get there. It couldn't just recall something from pretraining or do one quick search. Then we could use reinforcement learning on top of that, because we had a reliable way to say "yes, you got it" or "no, you didn't."

We also kept coming back to real usage. We'd ask what people wanted to delegate, like the tedious multi-tab research they'd spend an hour on, and use that to keep the tasks realistic, so we weren't just optimizing for a benchmark that didn't reflect how anyone would use the product. Those two pillars, verifiable hard tasks plus grounding in real user needs, guided most of our decisions early on.

r001.rationale: The response says the research was grounded in real user needs and tasks people would delegate, using realistic multi-tab research to reflect how people would use the product.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was something we thought about a lot when we started. With math and coding, there's this huge existing ecosystem: you have competition problems, you have GitHub, you have unit tests, you have ground truth answers that you can verify automatically. For browsing, none of that really existed. There's no "ImageNet for research tasks." So we had to be pretty deliberate about what we were actually optimizing for.

The first thing we did was just spend a lot of time thinking about what people actually want from a browsing agent. And the answer, at least for the kinds of use cases we cared about, was really hard research questions: things where you need to look at many sources, synthesize them, verify claims, and where the answer isn't on the first page of search results. So we tried to design tasks that had that character, rather than something like "find the capital of France," which the model can already do.

Then the second piece was verifiability. Even if you don't have an existing dataset, you still want a reward signal you can trust. So a lot of the early work was building tasks where there was a clear, checkable answer, even if the process of getting to it was long and open-ended. Sometimes that meant working backwards: start from a fact that's hard to find, and construct a question where the model would have to do real navigation and reasoning to get there. BrowseComp came out of that style of thinking, where the questions are deliberately hard to find but easy to verify once you have the answer.

And then honestly, a lot of it was just building the environments and tooling ourselves. We put a lot of effort into making the browsing environment robust, so the model could actually take hundreds of actions without things breaking, and so that when it failed, we could tell whether it was a model failure or an infrastructure failure. That's not glamorous, but it ended up being a big part of why the training worked.

The last thing I'd say is that we leaned on the fact that the model is a reasoning model. So even in cases where we didn't have perfect ground truth, we could use the model's own reasoning and some LLM-based grading to evaluate whether a research report was good, whether the claims were supported, whether it actually answered the question. That's noisier than a unit test, but for open-ended research, it ended up being a pretty reasonable signal, and it's gotten better as the models have gotten better.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they focused on what people wanted from a browsing agent and designed tasks around the research use cases they cared about.

astra-6.text:
We started by asking what people actually want to do with a browsing agent. Math and coding have these established datasets and fairly clear ways to check whether an answer is right. Browsing is much more open-ended, so choosing the tasks is itself a big part of the research.

We wanted to ground it in realistic things someone might delegate: finding information across several websites, comparing options with specific constraints, or pulling together information that isn’t all in one place. Then the question is, can we make those tasks concrete enough to evaluate? Did the agent actually find what was asked for, and does the information support its answer? That gives you a more useful starting point than just asking whether it can navigate a website.

r001.rationale: The response says the research was grounded in what people want a browsing agent to do and gives realistic tasks someone might delegate, conveying the intended product use cases.

sol-6.1.text:
We started by looking at what people actually wanted to do with a browsing agent. With math and coding, you have these existing datasets and fairly clear ways to check whether an answer is right. Browsing is much more open-ended, so we needed to build that foundation ourselves.

The approach was to collect realistic tasks—finding information across multiple sites, comparing options, answering questions that require some digging—and figure out what successful completion would look like. We wanted the research grounded in useful things people would actually delegate, with evaluations that could tell us whether the agent had really accomplished the task.

r001.rationale: The response says the research was grounded in realistic, useful tasks people would delegate to a browsing agent, conveying the product use cases the model was intended to handle.
